notes.b: Cream is the fat-rich layer separated from milk. Because nearly all the fat of the milk ends up in it, its nutrition is very different from that of milk, and its types differ mainly in how much fat they hold.
points: Cream is high in energy and contributes little protein or carbohydrate, because most of the protein and lactose (milk sugar) stay behind in the skimmed milk.
Its fat is mostly saturated and contains cholesterol, so cream is not suited to low-fat, low-cholesterol or slimming diets and is best used in small amounts.
The fat-soluble vitamins A and D are carried in the cream fat, because these vitamins dissolve in fat rather than water.
Cream contains no vitamin C and no fibre.
Double cream has the highest fat content (about 48%), whips to stiff peaks, pours thick and can be piped, so it suits fillings, toppings and rich sauces.
Single cream has less fat (about 18%), does not whip, and is used to pour over desserts, in coffee and in sauces.
Whipping cream (about 35 to 38% fat) is whipped to a foam by beating air into it, because the fat forms a network that traps the air.
Sour cream is cultured with lactic acid bacteria, giving a tangy flavour used in dips, toppings and baked potatoes. Crème fraîche is another cultured cream.
notes.tip: When asked for the nutritive value of cream or butter, say high in saturated fat and cholesterol, carries vitamins A and D, and has no vitamin C.

notes.b: Cream has to be separated from the milk, made to a set fat level and heat treated so that it is safe and keeps. Take care not to mix up separating cream with churning butter.
points: Cream is separated from milk by centrifugal separation (a spinning machine called a centrifuge), which spins the milk so the lighter fat rises and is drawn off. This separates cream from skimmed milk.
The fat content of each cream is standardised (adjusted) to the level named on the label, so that single, whipping and double cream are always the same.
The separated cream is then pasteurised or UHT treated, as for milk. UHT (long-life) cream keeps unopened without refrigeration.
After heat treatment the cream is cooled, packaged and labelled.
notes.tip: Centrifugal separation separates cream from skimmed milk. Churning separates butter from buttermilk. Do not swap the two.

notes.b: Cream is a perishable, high-fat food that absorbs smells easily, so choosing and storing it carefully protects its safety and flavour.
points: Select cream with the fat content stated on the label, which shows whether it is single, double or whipping cream and so whether it will whip or pour.
Check the use-by date and that the carton is intact and sealed.
Refrigerate cream promptly and keep it in its sealed container, away from strong-smelling foods, which it would otherwise absorb.
Once opened, use cream within the period stated on the label.
Whipped cream does not keep and should be used soon after whipping.
notes.tip: Selection and storage are asked in part answers: give the label (type and use-by date), a sealed carton, refrigeration and storing away from strong smells.

notes.b: Butter is made from cream by agitating it until the fat separates out. Because it is almost all fat, its nutritional profile follows the cream's.
points: Butter is made by churning (agitating) cream, which breaks down the membranes around the fat globules so the fat clumps together into butter grains.
The liquid left after churning is buttermilk. The butter is then washed, salted if wanted, worked (kneaded) to remove excess water, then shaped, wrapped and labelled.
Butter is about 80% fat (the EU minimum for the name butter) with a small amount of water, and its fat is mostly saturated.
Butter is high in cholesterol and supplies vitamins A and D from its fat. It has no vitamin C or fibre and negligible protein.
Salted butter has salt added for flavour and preservation, so unsalted butter suits those limiting salt.
Spreadable butter is blended with a vegetable oil to soften it. Reduced-fat spreads contain less fat because they are blended with other fats and water, and are chosen to reduce saturated fat.
A product with much less than 80% fat cannot legally be sold as butter, which is why lower-fat products are called reduced-fat spreads or dairy spreads.
notes.tip: Churning separates butter from buttermilk. Say reduced-fat spread for the lower-fat option, not a butter type.

notes.h: Culinary uses and storage of butter
notes.b: Butter is used for its flavour and for the way its fat behaves in cooking. It also picks up other smells easily, which shapes how it is stored.
points: Spreading on bread and toast.
Shortcrust and other pastry, where the fat is rubbed into the flour to make a crumbly (shortened) texture. Scones are made the same way.
Creaming with sugar in cake making, where air is beaten into the fat to aerate the mixture.
Frying and making sauces, such as white sauce or melted butter sauces, where it adds flavour. Butter burns at a lower heat than oil.
Butter is refrigerated, kept covered, and stored away from strong-smelling foods to prevent it absorbing odours.
Buy butter from a clean shop in intact packs, and use it before the use-by date. It can be frozen for long storage.
notes.tip: Butter uses examiners ask for are pastry, creaming and sauces. Link each use to what the fat does, such as shortening or aerating.

notes.b: Yoghurt is made from milk and so shares milk's nutrients, with the lactic acid making it easier to digest for many people.
points: Yoghurt supplies HBV protein (high biological value, with all the essential amino acids) for growth and repair.
Yoghurt supplies lactose as an energy source.
Yoghurt is rich in calcium and phosphorus for bones and teeth.
Yoghurt supplies vitamins A, D and B group vitamins.
Yoghurt is about 87% water, with traces of minerals such as potassium.
Full-fat yoghurt contains saturated fat, and yoghurt lacks vitamin C and is low in iron.
Dietetic value: yoghurt suits all ages, is versatile, can be fortified, is inexpensive and is a convenient snack.
Yoghurt is a cream substitute for those limiting cream's fat, and should be balanced with starch, fibre and iron foods, because it provides little of these.
notes.tip: Yoghurt is the most examined item here. Do not credit it with nutrients beyond those from milk unless it is fortified or has fruit added.

notes.b: Yoghurt is milk fermented by lactic acid bacteria: the bacteria change lactose to lactic acid, which gives the sharp taste, sets the milk and preserves it. The stages must be learned in order, with their temperatures.
points: 1. Milk is homogenised.
2. Milk is pasteurised at 80 to 90°C.
3. Milk is cooled to about 37°C, the temperature at which the culture can work.
4. A lactic culture such as Lactobacillus bulgaricus (usually with Streptococcus thermophilus) is added.
5. The mixture is incubated for 6 to 8 hours. Lactose changes to lactic acid, and the milk proteins coagulate (set) and thicken to form yoghurt.
6. The yoghurt is cooled to about 5°C to halt fermentation.
7. Sweeteners, fruit, nuts, colours, flavours or stabilisers may be added.
8. The yoghurt is weighed, packaged (in sealed plastic pots or cartons) and labelled.
notes.tip: Name the culture and give 80 to 90°C, 37°C, 6 to 8 hours and 5°C. In incubation, say lactose changes to lactic acid and the protein coagulates. Yoghurt is made with bacteria, not yeast, and the culture is added after pasteurisation, never before.

notes.h: Packaging, labelling and types of yoghurt
notes.b: Yoghurt is sold in sealed packs with a legal label, and it comes in several types depending on how it is set and what is added.
points: Yoghurt is packaged in sealed plastic pots with foil or plastic lids, or in cartons.
The label gives the name and type, brand, ingredients, quantity, nutrition information, allergens (milk, and any nuts), use-by date and storage (refrigerate).
The legal basis is Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
Set yoghurt is incubated in the pot and is firm. Stirred or drinking yoghurt is set in a vat, then stirred and poured into pots.
Greek-style yoghurt is strained and so thicker. Plain (natural) yoghurt has no sugar added.

notes.b: Bio-yoghurt has an extra live culture added for the consumer's benefit. How and when it is added matters, because heat would kill it.
points: Bio-yoghurt contains an added live culture such as Lactobacillus acidophilus, and bifidobacteria.
Acidophilus bacteria aid digestion, and help balance the bacteria in the gut.
Probiotic yoghurts contain live bacteria intended to benefit the gut. They must be refrigerated to stay alive.
The culture is added after pasteurisation, because heat would destroy it.
notes.tip: The benefit of acidophilus in bio-yoghurt is that it aids digestion. Stick to that wording and do not claim that probiotic yoghurt prevents or treats illness.

notes.b: Yoghurt is perishable and used in many ways, so choose and store it well and know a range of uses.
points: Buy from a clean shop, and check the use-by date and that the lid is sealed and the pot undamaged.
Check the ingredients list for sugar, fruit and possible allergens, and the origin of the product. Check the fat and sugar content on the label.
Refrigerate yoghurt promptly at about 4°C, rotate stock so older packs are used first, and reseal with the original lid. Use it within the time on the label.
Uses: eaten alone or as a drink, in desserts, salads and dressings, and smoothies.
Uses: as a garnish or topping, on cereal, as a dip (such as tzatziki or raita), and in curries, marinades and baking.
Yoghurt may replace cream or mayonnaise in cooking as a lower-fat option, but it curdles if boiled.
notes.tip: For a question on buying and storing yoghurt, give the use-by date, a sealed lid, the ingredients list and refrigeration. When choosing from a table, compare per 100 g for the lowest energy, saturated fat and salt, with protein for growth.

notes.h: Dairy industry responses to consumer trends
notes.b: Consumers want healthier, more convenient and more specialised dairy foods, so dairy producers change their products and packs. Each product change below answers a reason such as health awareness, convenience or intolerance.
points: Low-fat and skimmed products, including low-fat cheese and reduced-fat spreads, meet concern about obesity and heart disease.
Fortified products, such as milk with added vitamins, calcium or omega-3 fatty acids.
Functional yoghurts (foods with an added health benefit) with added probiotic cultures or plant stanol or sterol products.
Lactose-free, sugar-free and high-protein yoghurts, for people with lactose intolerance or following healthy eating guidelines.
Convenience formats: individually wrapped cheese portions, drinking yoghurts and frozen yoghurt.
Added-value products such as grated cheese and flavoured spreadable butter.
Extended shelf life through UHT treatment and aseptic packaging.
Resealable packs and varied sizes for family use.
notes.tip: Name at least three products and give the trend or reason each one answers. Linking each measure to its reason earns the marks.

keyTerms.definition: Agitating cream so that the fat globules break and clump together to form butter.
The liquid left after cream has been churned into butter.
Cream with the highest fat content, which whips to stiff peaks.
Lactic acid bacteria added to milk to convert lactose to lactic acid in products such as yoghurt and cheese.
Holding a culture-inoculated mixture at a constant warm temperature so the bacteria can multiply and ferment the milk.
A live micro-organism that, when eaten in sufficient amount, benefits the gut.
Yoghurt to which an additional culture such as Lactobacillus acidophilus has been added.
A food to which an ingredient has been added that is claimed to give a health benefit beyond basic nutrition.
Separating milk into cream and skimmed milk by spinning it at high speed, so the lighter fat rises.

questions.prompt: Explain the role of the lactic culture in yoghurt making and state the temperature at which it is added.
questions.model: The culture is added after the milk has been pasteurised and cooled to about 37°C. The lactic acid bacteria convert lactose into lactic acid, which gives yoghurt its sharp flavour and acts as a preservative. The acid causes the milk proteins to coagulate, thickening the mixture into yoghurt during incubation of 6 to 8 hours.

questions.prompt: Discuss the nutritional significance of yoghurt in the diet, and describe the guidelines to follow when buying and storing it.
questions.model: Nutritional significance: HBV protein for growth and repair; lactose and fat for energy; calcium and phosphorus for bones and teeth; vitamins A, D and B group; about 87% water; saturated fat in full-fat varieties; no vitamin C or iron, so it should be balanced with starch, fibre and iron foods. Dietetic value: suits all ages, versatile, digestible, fortifiable, inexpensive and convenient. Buying: clean shop, check use-by date and intact lid, check ingredients and allergens and origin. Storage: refrigerate promptly, rotate stock, reseal with the original lid and use by the date stated.
